outcome: No proof of existence or non-existence of a perfect cuboid has been accepted by the mathematical community since 26 January 2024; a large, uncoordinated wave of unreviewed preprints and Zenodo postings claiming non-existence proofs appeared through 2025-2026, alongside genuine incremental computational/theoretical progress (de Grey-Gibbs-Helm 2024, Asiryan 2025), but none has been digested, verified, or accepted, so the problem remains open as stated.

disputes.summary: Between roughly May 2025 and April 2026 at least six independent, mutually uncoordinated preprints/Zenodo postings (ResearchGate 'Simplified proof', Zenodo differential-algebraic-closure proof, arXiv:2602.00239 'An Elementary Obstruction', arXiv:2604.28072 'torsion-intersection proof on 1,072 fibers', a further Zenodo 'Mordell Weil Rank Exhaustion' posting, and others) each separately claim to prove non-existence of a perfect cuboid using unrelated methods, none citing or refuting the others, none appearing in a peer-reviewed venue, and none discussed in expert forums (no MathOverflow thread, no Terence Tao blog post, no journal acceptance found). This pattern (many disconnected 'complete proof' claims of a centuries-old problem posted to math.GM/Zenodo in quick succession) is itself the notable event, more than any single paper.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen statement covers existence of a perfect cuboid (integer edges, face diagonals, and space diagonal) and the associated 'cuboid conjectures'. Since 26 January 2024, no result has been accepted by the mathematical community: no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or MathOverflow/blog consensus was found for any claimed non-existence proof. What has happened is (a) genuine but modest incremental progress: de Grey, Gibbs and Helm's 'Novel required properties of, and efficient algorithms to seek, perfect cuboids' (arXiv:2401.06784, submitted 6 January 2024 — before the frozen revision, so this specific paper is background rather than in-window news, though its Geombinatorics journal appearance is dated 2024) extended computational search ranges and identified elliptic-curve families that must have positive rank if a perfect cuboid exists; and Valery Asiryan's October 2025 paper (arXiv:2510.11768) proved irreducibility of the cuboid polynomial in a two-parameter case, resolving 'Sharipov's first conjecture' as a special case rather than the full problem — this is a genuine `partial` result on a named sub-conjecture within the field, confirming the conjectured irreducibility. But (b) the dominant phenomenon in the window is a wave of unreviewed, mutually uncited preprints and Zenodo deposits (May 2025 through April 2026) each independently claiming to fully resolve non-existence via unrelated methods — divisor-based parameterization, differential algebraic closure, elementary congruence/descent arguments (Yelle, arXiv:2602.00239), and torsion-intersection arguments on 1,072 explicit fibers (Peschmann, arXiv:2604.28072, which itself only claims to prove the conjecture on fibers where max(a,b) ≤ 100, i.e. a bounded family, not the full conjecture, despite its abstract's 'unconditional proof' language). None of these has been checked by named experts, none appears accepted at a journal, and no retraction or rebuttal was found either — they simply sit uncorroborated. None discloses any AI/LLM involvement; the only computational tools mentioned (PARI's ellrank, Sage) are classical computer-algebra systems, not AI. A general essay on AI-generated mathematics (Weinreich, arXiv:2608.02859, August 2026) was found but does not mention perfect cuboids specifically and gives no evidence tying this particular flood to AI authorship. Given the absence of any accepted resolution, and treating the Peschmann/Yelle/ResearchGate claims individually as unverified preprints rather than established results, the correct status is `open`, not `claimed`, because §6.1 reserves `claimed` for a specific preprint or announcement that at least represents the field's live candidate outcome; here there are several mutually exclusive 'complete proof' candidates with no way to identify a single decisive one, and the Peschmann paper (the most-cited of the flurry) itself only covers a bounded fiber family rather than the whole conjecture. The closest thing to `partial` status is Asiryan's irreducibility result on Sharipov's first conjecture, but that is a named sub-conjecture in the broader 'cuboid conjectures' family rather than the existence question itself, so I record it in summary/disputes rather than driving the top-level status.
competing_reading: A stricter reading could set status to `claimed` keyed on arXiv:2604.28072 (Peschmann, 30 April 2026), since it is the most recent, most technically detailed, and most narrowly scoped ('1,072 explicit master-tuple fibers' bounded by max(a,b) ≤ 100) of the non-existence claims, and a triage record found it too. I did not adopt this because the paper's own scope is explicitly a bounded family of fibers, not the general conjecture, so even if fully correct it would only be `partial` at best, and with zero expert verification even `partial`/`claimed` status feels premature given several competing unverified claims exist with no way to adjudicate priority or correctness from outside. A reader who weights 'most recent, most technical' preprints more heavily than I do might instead file this as `claimed` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (i.e., confirming non-existence).
what_would_settle_it: Any of: an expert (e.g. a number theorist active in Diophantine geometry, or a MathOverflow/Tao-blog discussion) publicly assessing correctness of one of the 2025-2026 non-existence claims; acceptance of any of these preprints at a peer-reviewed journal; a formal Lean/Coq verification of the argument; or a rebuttal/counterexample showing one of the claimed proofs is flawed (which, given the volume of mutually silent claims, seems at least as likely as any one being correct).
